history.recommendation_text: The Board recommends that the Administration ensure that the Special Political Missions conduct a comprehensive analysis of the root causes for the significant variances between actual vehicle and computing devices holdings and standard allocations.
history.administration_response: The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) armoured passenger vehicle holding for 2024 is 149, excluding 10 vehicles earmarked for security use (close protection) and is therefore above the standard allocation of 96. In 2024, 17 vehicles will be written- off and 14 new vehicles are expected to arrive, bringing the total to 146 vehicles. The vehicle holdings at UNAMA are 52.0 per cent higher than the standard allocation and is attributable to the operational requirement for the allocation of 48 vehicles in the dispatch pool across all the regions of the Mission for airport shuttle services, road missions and 2 driver testing vehicles. The UNAMA armoured vehicle holding is based on the assessed security situation where the elevated use of armoured vehicles is dictated by the extant security threats. All staff transportation is in armoured vehicles and every road mission requires a minimum of two vehicles with a maximum of three passengers (with personal protective equipment) per vehicle. The interior space of an armoured vehicle is reduced after the up-armouring process, which should also be taken into consideration. With regards to ICT equipment, at the end of December 2023, the total holding was 1,236 computing devices, exceeding the authorized number of 1,196. This surplus is attributed to delays in the delivery of newly ordered equipment, in customs clearance with the de facto authorities and in the process of writing off old devices. Consequently, the inventory of ICT devices is projected to increase further until the delivery of equipment to UNAMA custody, the implementation of a full replacement programme and completion of the write- off process. We anticipate that this issue will be addressed and resolved by the first quarter of 2025. The Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) has undertaken an inventory of computing devices to reflect the actual holding within the department. The Security Council Committee had 20 laptops assigned to it in 2023, of which four will be disposed of by June 2024, 16 laptops are in current use by 9 non-staff experts, including one common laptop in the conference room for the Group of Experts, and by 5 support staff, and 1 laptop has been transferred within the Office for Disarmament Affairs.
history.board_assessment: Given that the analysis of the root causes is still in process, the Board considers this recommendation to be under implementation.

history.entities_raw: Office for Disarmament Affairs, Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria, United Nations Office for West Africa and the Sahel, United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia, UNMSIL, United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), United Nations Integrated Transition Assistance Mission in the Sudan, Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region and UNAMA
history.sg_progress: Following a comprehensive review, the Office for Disarmament Affairs conducted an accurate inventory of computing devices as identified by the Board. The inventory revealed the following: (a) outdated units, which are now scheduled for decommissioning; (b) units assigned to staff members and non-staff experts of the Security Council resolution 1540 support unit; and (c) a unit designated for a conference room. With the disposal process nearing completion, the support unit will achieve the standard device-to-user ratio. The number of computers at BINUH is maintained at the standard 1:1 ratio, in accordance with the Standard Cost and Ratio Manual. Additional computers are kept as spares and issued to staff on the basis of operational requirements, including running the Autocard software, CarLog system, training purposes, Field Technology Services presentations, radio programming, server maintenance and software monitoring. In 2024, BINUH vehicle holdings exceed the standard allocation by 12 units owing to: (a) the operational need for a pool of duty vehicles for medical, security, information technology and engineering personnel to respond swiftly to emergencies; (b) frequent maintenance and repairs necessitated by poor road conditions and prolonged repair durations at outsourced workshops; and (c) the requirement for driver testing vehicles. In 2025, BINUH is projected to exceed the standard allocation by only four units, reflecting an improvement from the previous period. UNSMIL maintains a fleet of 11 vehicles in eastern Libya to support its operations. This arrangement mitigates security risks and transportation costs associated with moving the fleet from west to east. Given the volatile security situation in Libya, the Mission exercises an exception to deviate from the standard vehicle holding ratio. This deviation is essential to ensure business continuity across all locations in Libya while minimizing security risks to staff and United Nations assets. With respect to computing devices, the Mission has initiated replacements, subject to necessary clearances from the host Government. The Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region maintains an inventory of computing devices that includes those used by consultants, devices maintained as spares and tablets issued to staff on the basis of operational requirements. The current inventory has decreased compared with the December 2022 actual holding owing to the disposal of 21 devices in 2023. The Office plans to conduct a further review of its inventory and write off additional devices in 2024.

history.recommendation_text: The Board recommends that the Administration ensure that the Special Political Missions conduct a comprehensive analysis of the root causes for the significant variances between actual vehicle and computing devices holdings and standard allocations.
history.administration_response: Office for Disarmament Affairs: By the end of 2024, the disposal of four laptops had been processed and the laptops had been moved to the stockroom of the Office of Information and Communications Technology. United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA): The difference between actual computing devices and standard allocations stems from the following factors: (a) the holding of higher number of devices occurs because some functional areas receive shared or common-use devices, which include training rooms, radio rooms and conference rooms, Internet cafés, security gates and system monitoring facilities. In addition, the process of finding suitable recipients for personal laptop equipment has caused a delay in the write-off and disposal of such equipment. UNAMA has taken corrective action to resolve this situation. UNAMA retrieved 90 per cent of the surplus laptops assigned to staff members. The Mission has started the process of writing off 296 computing devices, while another 250 intended for disposal will be retrieved until suitable beneficiaries can be found. The Mission is implementing these measures to align the holdings of computing devices with the authorized holdings. United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL): The Mission has 11 armoured vehicles and 1 ambulance, totalling 12 vehicles, in eastern Libya. The UNSMIL administration continues to monitor the security conditions diligently and adapts its strategies in order to maintain operational effectiveness, while prioritizing the safety of its personnel and assets. The host Government has released the computing devices, and the obsolete laptops are gradually being replaced. The write-off and replacement process is expected to be completed by the end of 2025.

history.recommendation_text: In paragraph 63 of its report, the Board recommended that the Administration ensure that the special political missions conduct a comprehensive analysis of the root causes for the significant variances between actual vehicle and computing devices holdings and standard allocations.
history.reference_raw: Report of the Board for the year ended 31 December 2022 8
history.entities_raw: Office for Disarmament Affairs, BINUH, United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), United Nations Office for West Africa and the Sahel, Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria, and Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary- General for the Great Lakes Region
history.sg_progress: The Administration requests the closure of this recommendation by the Board on the basis of the following considerations: (a) Clarification was required by the Board regarding the methodology used to calculate the device-to-staff ratio. The Administration notes that the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) includes a significantly large number of experts – nearly double the number of supporting United Nations Secretariat staff. Each expert, in the same way as staff members, is assigned a dedicated laptop for daily work and travel. It was therefore necessary to confirm whether experts and other consultancy positions with assigned laptops should be included in the total staff count. This discrepancy is the primary factor contributing to the elevated device-to-staff ratio; (b) Due to recurring hardware issues identified in the most recent laptop procurement, the Support Unit in the Office for Disarmament Affairs has retained several older laptops as backup devices. The older laptops are used to ensure continuity of service when defective laptops are returned to the manufacturer for repair, a process that typically takes two weeks to one month; (c) Some devices are designated for shared use in conference rooms and are not assigned to individual staff members, which affects the calculated ratio. In addition, in line with current financial constraints, the Administration prioritizes the use of out-of-warranty but still functional equipment over new purchases, as part of broader cost-saving measures. UNAMA has retrieved 44 surplus laptops previously assigned to staff and has initiated the write-off process for devices that have exceeded their operational life. In addition, the Mission has completed the laptop replacement programme, resulting in the replacement of all outdated laptops. As of August 2025, the Mission operated a fleet of 156 vehicles, including 10 for close protection. In 2022, the holding of armoured passenger vehicles was 173. The vehicle fleet is assessed regularly for age, mileage and condition, with the aim of extending the operational useful life where possible. About 54 per cent of the fleet exceeds the 12-year life expectancy but the vehicles are in operational condition. These aged vehicles are used for passenger transportation and logistical requirements and will be phased out as they become unserviceable, which contributes to the higher-than-standard ratio of armoured vehicles when using light passenger vehicle calculations. Another factor to be considered is the security requirement for all staff to be transported in armoured vehicles, with strict security protocols such as a minimum of two vehicles per convoy, personnel protective equipment and a maximum of three passengers per vehicle.
